title: Chapter 59 – The Last Debt
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

They carry him out of the Orchard at dawn, on a door.

It is the cellar door, the old oak one, torn from its hinges by Wenshi's men and carried down into the dark. Four of the guards bear it, two to a side, and Jian lies on it with his head on a rolled cloak and a blanket to his chin and his eyes shut. He is not asleep. He is only very far away. He has been far away for some hours. It is a quiet, flat, gray place, a little like the inside of a cloud, and it has the great virtue of making the pain very small.

He hears them. It is the odd thing. He hears them from a long distance, as through a wall, in a ringing silence with a high thin note in it. His left ear is gone. His right is a dull shell. He hears Wenshi's voice, short and gruff, saying mind the step. He hears the creak of the stair. He hears, somewhere above and behind, a sound he has not heard in days, a great murmuring, a sound like wind in barley: three hundred and sixty-eight people coming up out of the earth into the light, and not saying a word.

Pebble is on his chest.

She is not moving. She lies curled in the hollow of his collar, small and bare and light as a dry leaf, and her breath, against his throat, is a faint slow flutter, like a moth beating at a window. She has not spoken since the pool. He has asked her, over and over, with the whole of his tired mind, and she has answered with a single wordless warmth, like a hand laid on his, that says only: tired. Not yet.

Not yet, he thinks. Not yet. Not yet.

It is a kind of prayer. It is the only one he knows.

* * *

The sun is up when they set him down.

It is a hard clear morning, with a high pale sky and a cold wind out of the north, and he opens his eyes to find the whole of the courtyard laid out in light. It is a ruin. The great paving has gone, a long broken trench of black slag and splintered stone, and across it, in rows, under white cloths, lie the dead. He counts them without wishing to. Sixty-four in the trench. Seven by the gate. Nine along the base of the great stair, with the cloth drawn over their faces, and a row of boots.

Not all of them are Red Ridge.

Thirty-one of ours, says the cold part of him, with great exactness. Thirty-one on the stair.

He does not look for names. He cannot. He lies very still, with the blanket to his chin, and lets the sun lie on his face, and the wind pluck at his hair. After a time a shadow falls across him, and he turns his head.

It is his father.

He is standing at the foot of the door, in a cloak of someone else's, with a blackened sword in one hand and a bandage round the other. His gray hair is matted with soot. There is a long raw cut across his cheek, still wet. He is swaying a little, as a tired man sways, and his face, under the grime, is the color of tallow. He looks about a hundred years old.

"Son," says Wenyuan.

His voice is quite quiet. It does not break. He kneels, very slowly, with one hand on the blade for a support, and takes his son's face between his two hands, and looks at it, for a long time, in the clear light.

"I am here," says Jian. It comes out as a croak. "I did not hear the horn."

"No. You would not have." The Patriarch's thumb moves, very gently, across his cheekbone. "It is all right. It is over. The old man is dead. Hu told me." A thin ghost of a smile. "He told me with a good deal of language."

"Mu."

"Yes."

"I killed him."

"I know."

"I did not want to."

"I know that too."

They stay like that for a moment, the man and the boy, in the cold bright wind, among the dead. Then the Patriarch lowers his head, and lays his forehead against his son's, and stays there, without speaking, until Jian feels the wetness on his own face and realizes that it is not only his.

* * *

The Arbiter comes at noon.

He does not come as an Arbiter should. There is no banner, no escort, no sedan. He rides up the Salt Road on a gaunt black horse, with a single groom behind him, in a plain gray robe covered with dust, and he gets down at the great gate, which still hangs on one hinge, and stands for a long time with the reins in his hand, looking at the ruin.

Jian sees him from the steps of the hall, where they have laid him on a pallet in the shade. He has been given a bowl of broth, which he has not touched, and a cup of Hu's tea, which he has. A thin gray man in a gray robe is standing in the broken gateway, quite alone, with the cold sun on his face.

He is not what Jian expected. He had thought, from the name, a great stern figure: a man of weight, with a long sword and a longer beard. He is neither. He is lean, middle-aged, rather bent, with a gaunt, ascetic face and iron-gray hair cropped close to the skull. He looks like a man who has been a clerk for thirty years and has never once enjoyed it. His eyes are small, and very dark, and extraordinarily tired.

Shen Wuye, thinks Jian. The Arbiter of the Outer Court. Mid Foundation.

Behind him, with a bundle under one arm and a face of studied blankness, rides a second figure, a lean sallow man in a traveling robe, on a stolid gray gelding.

Cheng Yun.

He had written the letter. It had gone in the Inspector's own saddlebag, on the fourth, four days before the new moon. To the Arbiter, from the Patriarch of Green Pine, in the matter of a certain compact between Red Ridge and the Blood Shadow. It had been eight pages. It had been, his father said, the best thing he had ever written.

And it got here, he thinks, with a faint dull wonder. In time.

"Patriarch Lin," says the Arbiter.

His voice is quite soft. It is a dry, level, exhausted voice, without any inflection at all. He has walked across the courtyard, between the rows of white cloths, with his hands folded in his sleeves, and he has stopped at the foot of the hall steps, and he does not look at the dead. He looks only at Wenyuan.

"Arbiter." Wenyuan has risen. He is bowing, stiffly, from the waist, with the bandaged hand held against his chest. "You are most welcome. I regret the state of the house."

"I have seen worse." The small dark eyes travel over him, from the cut on his cheek to the blackened sword, slowly, without haste. "You wrote that you expected an attack on the new moon of the seventh month."

"Yes."

"You wrote that it would be a joint action of the Red Ridge clan and the Blood Shadow Sect, in violation of the Treaty of the Eastern Marches."

"Yes."

"I regret," says Shen Wuye, "that I was a day late."

"You were a night late. I would not have it otherwise." Wenyuan's mouth twists, very slightly. "The writ came before the wolves. It is the only reason I have a hill."

The Arbiter regards him a moment longer. Then he turns, and surveys the courtyard once, slowly: the trench, and the slag, and the long white rows, and the broken wall. It is a thorough survey. It misses nothing.

"Who commanded the Red Ridge?" he says.

* * *

It is Zhao Heng who answers.

He has been brought in at the gate by his own men. There are four of them left, ragged, gray-faced, with their hands bound, and they carry the long black lacquer chair between them like a coffin. He sits in it quite upright, in a robe of dark red silk, with a fur across his knees. He is thinner than Jian remembers. He is much older. His face is a mask of old yellow wax, with two black coals for eyes, and he looks round the broken courtyard with the cool deliberate attention of a man appraising a field.

He has not run, thinks Jian. He could have. They all ran. He stayed.

"I commanded it," says Heng.

The voice is faint and dry and very distinct. It carries across the whole of the yard. The men at the foot of the stair turn their heads.

"Zhao Heng, Patriarch of Red Ridge." The Arbiter has not moved. "You are accused of conspiring with a proscribed sect, of the Blood Shadow, to commit an armed assault on a registered clan of the Outer Court, in the season of the Register, without an Arbiter's writ. How do you answer?"

"I answer," says Heng, "that I wish to make a claim."

There is a small shocked silence.

"A claim?"

"Under the Founder's Precept, section nine." The cracked voice is steady. "Where a registered clan holds, on its land, a work of the Sect's Founder, it shall declare the same to the Outer Court, and the Court shall hold it in trust. I have reason to believe that the Lin clan of Green Pine has failed to so declare." He lifts one thin hand. "I have reason to believe that under the quarry of this hill there lies a door."

Jian does not breathe.

He had known it would come. He has known since the quarry, since a thin sallow man had stood at the foot of the east wall in the evening light and put out his hand. But it is a different thing to hear it said, in the plain cold air, before the Arbiter of the Outer Court, by a man who is dying in a chair.

He is gambling, he thinks. He has nothing left. The cure is dead. The donor is dead. The siege has failed, and Mu is in two pieces at the bottom of a hole, and he is going to be tried for treason in a Sect court. He has one chip.

He is going to put it on the table.

"It is a very serious charge," says the Arbiter, without expression.

"It is a very serious door." Heng's black eyes move, slowly, across the courtyard, across the white cloths, across the Patriarch in his stained cloak. They come to rest, at last, on the boy on the pallet in the shade. "And I can prove it."

"How?"

"I have a Root-Seeking Mirror."

Nobody speaks.

"It is the Sect's own. It was lent to my house in the spring, for the testing of the children. It reads the five roots, and the stage, and the hidden thing under both. It does not lie." The thin lips curve. "I should like, Arbiter, with your leave, to put it to one child. And let the Court see what it says."

* * *

They bring it out on a tray.

It is a small thing: a disc of bronze, no larger than a man's palm, set in a frame of black wood. The face is polished, and dark, and absolutely smooth. It has no light in it. It is simply a surface, like a pool at night, and when Zhao Bei lifts it from its cloth and holds it in two hands, the sun does not shine on it. It drinks the light.

Jian has seen it before. In the spring, in the schoolhouse, on a gray winter morning, he had stood in a line of children and put his hand on the cold bronze, and it had shown nothing. It had shown an empty dark. It had shown him, as he was, with a thin gray Veil laid over his thoughts like a dust sheet over furniture, and had looked at the Veil, and seen only that there was nothing under it.

It cannot read what I have not got, he had thought.

But he has not got the Veil. It is gone. It lies in a hundred silver scraps at the bottom of a dark pool, and in its place there is only a raw bright place in the center of his mind, like a tooth that has been drawn.

I have nothing to hide behind.

He thinks it quite calmly. It is a strange thing. He has been afraid of the Mirror for a year. Now that it is here, on a tray, in the sun, in the hands of a gray-faced man in scorched leather, he finds that the fear has gone out of him, as a fever goes. In its place there is only a sort of vast, clear, tired courtesy.

Well, he thinks. Here it is.

"The boy is hurt," says Wenyuan.

"The boy is nineteen years old, and he has been called a prodigy by half the Ford." Heng's voice is mild. "I should hardly think a hurt boy would be less honest than a well one."

"He is my son."

"I know it." The dark eyes turn, slowly, toward the Patriarch. They hold, a long moment, a thing that Jian cannot read, a bleak dry gleam, as of a man looking at the last coin in his purse. "I have never doubted it. It is why I have waited so long."

"Arbiter," says Wenyuan.

Shen Wuye has not moved. He stands in the sun with his hands in his sleeves and his small tired eyes on the little bronze disc.

"The claim is made under the Precept," he says, at last. "I am bound to hear it." He turns his head, a very little. "Young master. Will you permit it?"

Jian lies for a moment in the shade with the blanket to his chin.

Then he puts it back. He sits up. It is not easy. His ribs grind, and his left side is numb, and the ringing in his head is like a hammer on a sheet of tin. But he gets his feet over the edge of the pallet, and then his hands, and he stands, swaying a little, in the cold bright wind, and holds out his right hand, palm up.

"Yes," he says.

* * *

It is very cold.

He has expected that. The bronze is the temperature of deep water. It lies in his palm like a coin dropped through ice, and for a long moment there is nothing at all. The Arbiter is watching him, motionless. Heng is watching him, with a faint terrible smile. Behind him, he can feel the whole of the courtyard hold its breath.

Then the Mirror wakes.

It does not flash. It deepens. The black face of the disc grows darker, and darker, a long soft sinking, until it seems to him that he is looking down a well. And at the bottom of the well, far away, small and clear, a light comes up.

It is green. It is gold. It is red, and white, and the deep still blue of a river at night. It is five colors, all at once, burning in a ring, like five small flames in a wind, and they do not flicker. They are steady. They are bright. They are, he sees, in a strange cold flash of recognition, his.

Five elements.

A gasp goes through the courtyard.

The flames grow. They lean toward each other, slowly, like five children who have been told to join hands, and where they meet, in the center of the ring, a darkness appears. It is small. It is round. It is the size of a grain of rice, and it hangs in the heart of the fire like a seed in the heart of a fruit.

And over it, quite distinctly, in a clear white line, as a clerk might write on the bottom of a ledger, the Mirror says:

FIVE-ELEMENT ROOT. QI REFINING, STAGE EIGHT. AGE: NINETEEN.

SEED: PRESENT. SEED: NOT OF THIS SECT.

Not of this sect.

He stares at the words. He does not know what they mean. It is some old formula, he thinks, the Mirror's own, a tag for what it cannot place. But he sees, out of the corner of his eye, the lean figure of the Arbiter go quite still, and he sees Cheng Yun, behind him, take a short sharp breath.

"Stage eight," says Shen Wuye, softly.

"At ten," says Heng. He sounds almost gentle. "It is a most remarkable stage. It is not a thing that is done. And a five-element root has not been known to pass the third in six hundred years." The thin hand lifts, at last, and points. "He has taken it from the door, Arbiter. The thing under the quarry. I do not know how. But I think, if you ask him, he will tell you that it is not a method of any known school."

"It is called," says Jian, quite clearly, "the Five Seasons Seed Canon."

He had not meant to say it. It is out before he has thought. He stands with the bronze in his palm and his hand shaking, and the words fall into the silence like stones.

"Half of it," he says. "The other half is missing. It was in the Orchard, under the hill. I found it three months ago. I have the original in a place I will not name, and a copy in my head." He swallows. "The Orchard is a small garden. It is a remnant. It has a pool, and a hundred herbs, and eleven Wardens. It cannot make a sect. It can keep a clan alive." He lifts his chin. "That is what the door is. That is all."

Nobody moves.

"Why have you told me this?" says the Arbiter, at last, very quietly.

"Because it is true."

"It will cost you the garden."

"Yes."

"And the Canon."

"Yes." He looks at the lean gray face in the sun. "I would rather lose them than be a thing that has to be hidden."

* * *

For a long time the Arbiter does not answer.

He stands in the cold light with his small dark eyes on the boy, and his face does not change. It is a gaunt, tired, bone-colored face. It might be a carving. And then, very slowly, as a man might who has seen a thing he did not know he had been waiting for, he turns his head, and looks at Heng.

"Patriarch Zhao."

"Arbiter."

"You have made a claim under the ninth section of the Founder's Precept. It is a valid claim. The Court will examine it." The dry voice does not alter. "You have also, in the course of making it, confessed before witnesses that you knew of the door for a year, and did not declare it. You have confessed that you tested the Lin heir with a Sect instrument, in secret, without writ. You have confessed that you conspired with the Elder of the Well to take it."

"I did not—"

"The four dead men in the quarry wear the bone masks of the Pool." The Arbiter's eyes do not leave his face. "Inspector Cheng has examined them. I have seen the ash of the Blood Shadow's own men on the northern slope, in the ledger of a month ago. I have seen the letter you sent to the Lin Elder Zhong, which the Inspector took from his study at dawn." A very faint, very dry pause. "It is a charming letter. It has your signature on it."

Heng's face is quite blank.

"I am not a vindictive man," says Shen Wuye. "I have been Arbiter of the Outer Court for nineteen years. I do not enjoy it. But I know a gambler when I see one, and I know when a man has put his last coin on a table and found it lead." He turns, a little, to the lean figure behind him. "Inspector."

"Arbiter."

"Draft the order."

Cheng Yun bows. He draws a brush from his sleeve. And in the cold bright silence of the broken courtyard, in the middle of the dead, the Arbiter of the Outer Court says, in a voice like a dry leaf on stone:

"By the authority of the Court, the House of Red Ridge is stripped of its seat at the Register, and its lands are placed under the Court's hand. Its Patriarch is remanded to the Outer Court, in his chair, for trial. Its steward, one Zhao Bei, is to answer for the deaths at the Lin hall." He pauses. "And its heir, the girl called Zhao Qian, is to be taken into the custody of the Court, in the care of the Inspector, until a guardian is named."

There is a very small sound.

It is not a gasp. It is a thin short breath, like the sound of a held cord parting. Jian turns his head, and sees, at the foot of the great stair, among the bound men, a small stiff figure in dark red, with her right hand in a black silk glove. She has not moved. Her face is a perfect blank. But the glove is shaking, a fine, fast, continual tremor, as a leaf shakes in a gale.

She is not afraid, he thinks, with a sudden sick clarity. She is not afraid. She is relieved.

It is a terrible thing to see.

* * *

They take Heng away in the afternoon.

It is not a spectacle. They carry him out through the broken gate in the black lacquer chair, with a clerk on either side, past the long white rows and the weeping women and the old schoolmaster, standing very straight, with his book against his chest. He does not look round. He sits perfectly upright, in his red silk, with the fur across his knees, and when he reaches the Salt Road, at the foot of the slope, he lifts one hand, slowly, to shield his eyes from the sun.

At the very last, he turns his head.

He does not look at the Patriarch. He does not look at the hall. He looks, across two hundred paces of cold bright air, directly at the boy on the steps.

It is not a hateful look. It is not a hungry one. It is only a long steady stare, from a pair of black dry eyes in a face of yellow wax, and in it, very faintly, quite clearly, Jian reads a thing he did not expect. It is a sort of weary, rueful, almost tender recognition, as of a man who has found, at the end of a long road, the one person on earth who understands why he came.

Then the chair goes round the bend, and is gone.

* * *

It is Hu who finds him, in the evening, on the steps.

He has been sitting there since the dusk began, with the blanket round his shoulders and a cup of cold tea in his hands. The courtyard is dark. A few lanterns burn along the wall. Somewhere in the lower yard a woman is singing, very low, a long slow dirge in the old mountain mode, and the wind has dropped, and the first stars are coming out above the broken roofs.

The old refiner lowers himself onto the step beside him. His knees crack. He does not speak for a while.

"You are shaking," he says at last.

"It is the cold."

"It is not the cold." Hu's voice is dry and gentle. "I have been shaking for six days. It is the thing a man does when he has been very brave for too long. It passes."

"Does it?"

"No." A small silence. "But you learn to stand in it."

They sit side by side, in the dark, with the lanterns blinking along the wall, and for a while neither says anything at all. Hu's one hand lies on his knee. It is trembling, a very fine fast tremor, the old fever-shake of the Veiled Forge's last fire, the thing that has haunted him for twenty-nine years. Jian has watched it, in the granary, in the cold gray mornings, as it passes through the long gnarled fingers and into the bent rod, and he has never once asked.

Level 3, he thinks. Separation. Living tissue.

He looks at the hand.

It will not give him the arm, he thinks, with a small cold ache. It will not give him anything back. It will only take away the thing that was put there.

He thinks about it for a long time. In the dark a bat goes over, a quick small shadow, silent as a thought.

"Hu."

"Mm?"

"May I take your hand?"

The old man looks at him. In the starlight his one clear eye is dark and bright and very steady. He says nothing at all. He only lifts the hand, the shaking one, and lays it in the boy's two small palms, as a man lays down a sword.

Yes, thinks Jian.

It is very quiet. It is very quick. A thin pale thread, not red this time but gray, the color of old ash, comes out of the old man's wrist and trails away into the dark, and is gone. And the hand in his, which has trembled for twenty-nine years, becomes, under his fingers, for the first time since he has known it, entirely still.

Hu does not move. He lies there with his palm open on the boy's knee, looking at it, as a man looks at a thing he has dreamed. He turns it over. He flexes the fingers, slowly, one by one. He holds it up, in the starlight, in front of his face, and looks at it, for a very long time.

"Ah," he says. It is almost nothing. It is the sound a man makes who has put down a heavy bag at the end of a long road. "Ah."

"I could not give you the arm."

"I know." Hu's voice is thick. "I did not ask. I never asked. I have never once in my life asked for the arm."

"I know."

"I asked for this." He closes his hand. He opens it. It does not shake. "I did not know that I had."

He puts his single arm round the boy, awkwardly, hard, with the stubble of his beard against Jian's hair, and holds him, in the dark, on the broken steps of the hall, while far off in the lower yard the woman's dirge goes on, low and slow, and the stars come out, one by one, over a hill that is still, for another year, a hill.
